faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Camden basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In Camden's rowhouses the signs concentrate in the basement kitchens and rear additions, and the run usually enters where the old sewer and water lines pass through the foundation. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: There is a dead-animal smell in my Camden house but I can't find anything — can you?
faqs.a: Yes — locating it is a method, not a guess. Smell intensity, fly activity, and the floor plan narrow it to a wall void, a crawlspace corner, or a stretch of ductwork, and we open the smallest section that lets us remove the carcass. Camden's flat-roofed porch additions hide carcasses well; a raccoon that dies in a porch roof void perfumes the whole front of the house before anyone finds the entry it used. The spot then gets disinfected and deodorized, and we check how the animal got in, because a carcass in a wall usually means an entry that is still open. Carcasses of rabies-vector species are handled with gloves and bagged, never bare-handed.

Camden.wildlife_intro:
Camden's housing is the oldest urban stock in South Jersey: brick rowhouses and twins in Parkside and Whitman Park, frame homes in Cramer Hill, and the garden-suburb streets of Fairview, all of it threaded by the Cooper River and backed by the Delaware waterfront. Norway rats are the city's defining wildlife call, entrenched in the older blocks, the sewer laterals, and the vacant-lot edges. Raccoons are a close second, denning in porch roofs and the chimneys of houses that have sat empty, and starlings and sparrows fill the vents of the commercial corridors.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. In Camden a sealed unit beside an open, vacant one is a temporary fix, so our inspections note the condition of the adjoining rooflines and say plainly what that means for the result.

faqs.q: Why can't I get an exact wildlife quote for my Cherry Hill home over the phone?
faqs.a: Because the same scratching sound can mean a short fix or a colony that has been overhead for two seasons — nobody honest can price it from a description. A Barclay Farm cape with one squirrel-chewed gable and a Woodcrest colonial with a raccoon litter and a fouled attic are both common Cherry Hill calls, and they price very differently. After the inspection you hold a written figure covering removal, entry sealing, and cleanup, and the work does not begin until you approve it.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Cherry Hill garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. The stream-corridor lots in Springdale and Ellisburg give groundhogs banked, brushy den sites a short walk from vegetable gardens, which is why the burrow, not the garden fence, is the target. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

Cherry Hill.wildlife_intro:
Cherry Hill grew in one great postwar wave, and its Barclay Farm capes, Woodcrest split-levels, and Ashland colonials now sit under a half-century of oak and pine canopy along the Cooper River's north branch. That canopy is the story: squirrels bridge from limb to roofline on street after street, raccoons raise litters in the chimneys of the older sections, and groundhogs colonize the stream corridors and the big rear lots in Ellisburg and Springdale. Bats take the quieter attics near the river parkland every summer.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Cherry Hill proofing starts with a tape measure between limb and roofline, because on these streets the tree work is frequently half the animal work.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Voorhees Township lawn at night and it smells like skunk — what is going on?
faqs.a: Neat, cone-shaped holes in turf mean a skunk is mining grubs and earthworms, and late winter adds mating-season scent to the picture. Around Voorhees' ponds and irrigated commons the grub hunting is excellent, and the cone-holing often appears in a ring around the same few streets in the same week. The lasting answer is removing the den site and the food: we clear any skunk sheltering under steps or sheds, screen those voids, and talk through grub-heavy turf, because a lawn full of larvae gets visited nightly no matter how many skunks are taken off it.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Voorhees Township ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. The Echelon-area colonials give squirrels a familiar target: the junction where a garage roof meets the main wall, a joint that opens as the two structures settle differently. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

Voorhees Township.wildlife_intro:
Voorhees is a township of planned subdivisions and office-park greenery: Kresson's older homes, the Echelon area's townhouses and colonials, and big newer houses around Kirkwood and the Gibbsboro border. Stafford Farm's open ground and the township's many retention ponds and wooded buffers keep wildlife threaded through all of it. Raccoons and squirrels work the rooflines, skunks dig the irrigated lawns around the ponds, groundhogs take the field edges, and bats settle into the attics of the quieter cul-de-sacs each June.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. Voorhees yards back onto ponds, buffers, and farm fields in every direction, so the yard survey here covers the lot line and what lives just past it.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my Gloucester Township attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. Blackwood's older homes produce Gloucester Township's classic version of this call: a raccoon through a rotted eave, a litter in the insulation, and a ceiling stain as the first announcement. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

faqs.q: Once the animals are out of my Gloucester Township home, how do I keep them out?
faqs.a: Walk the house the way an animal does: roofline first, then vents, then ground level. Chimney cap, metal-backed vent covers, limbs cut back off the roof, trash in lidded cans, and no pet food or open seed stored in the garage. Erial's newer homes sit close to Barrens woods, so the fall checklist there leans on vent covers and garage seals, the two places new construction leaves soft. We leave you the entry map from your own job — which gaps were sealed and which aging spots to watch — because the houses that stay quiet are checked each fall, not just fixed once.

Gloucester Township.wildlife_intro:
Gloucester Township is really several communities sharing a tax map: Blackwood's older village streets, Glendora and Chews Landing's postwar blocks, Blenheim's small homes, and Erial's newer subdivisions pushing toward the Winslow pines. The housing runs from century-old frame homes near the old Blackwood lake district to vinyl-sided colonials built last decade. Raccoons and squirrels are universal; the southern and eastern edges, where lots meet Barrens woods, add groundhogs, skunks, and the occasional pine snake report from a woodpile.

Garages and sheds are the soft underbelly of a property. A garage door that stops a quarter-inch high, a shed set straight on soil, stored birdseed and grass seed in open bags — raccoons, rats, skunks, and opossums all read that as an invitation. Proofing means door sweeps and corner seals on the garage, hardware-cloth skirts on the shed, and feed and seed moved into lidded metal bins. Many house infestations turn out to start in the garage and commute through a shared attic or a breezeway, so the outbuildings get inspected with the house, every time. In Gloucester Township's subdivisions the garage is the usual beachhead, and outbuilding proofing is written into the plan alongside the house work.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Pennsauken Township home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. Pennsauken rats commute from the riverfront and rail edges along fence lines and ivy, and the houses that stay clear are the ones with mortared entries, lidded cans, and nothing edible stored at ground level. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Pennsauken Township deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. Pennsauken's porches sit low over damp ground near two rivers, and an opossum family under the front steps is one of the township's most routine spring calls. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

Pennsauken Township.wildlife_intro:
Pennsauken sits between the Delaware River and the Cooper River with a century of industry and postwar housing layered together: older twins and capes near Merchantville, brick homes in the Delaware Gardens area, and working riverfront blocks where warehouses meet residential streets. Rats are the headline here, commuting between the riverfront industry, the rail lines, and the houses behind them. Raccoons work the Cooper River corridor and the older chimneys, opossums den under porches across town, and starlings fill the vents along the commercial strips.

Food decides where animals settle. Bird feeders spill seed that feeds rats at night, pet dishes sit out on porches, trash waits in cans a raccoon can open in seconds, and fallen fruit ferments under backyard trees. Removal without changing that menu is a short truce. We go over the property's food map with the homeowner — secured cans, feeders on baffled poles set away from the house, fruit picked up, grills cleaned — because the houses that stay quiet are the ones that stop advertising. The animal work and the housekeeping have to happen together. Pennsauken jobs come with a frank conversation about dumpsters and back-lot food sources, because the riverfront blocks will re-stock a careless property indefinitely.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my Haddonfield attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. Haddonfield's big Victorian attics are maternity roosts by June in many cases, so summer callers here get a documented survey and a place in the August exclusion schedule rather than a rushed job. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

faqs.q: What makes one Haddonfield wildlife job cost more than another?
faqs.a: Access, animal count, and aftermath. A steep roof, a maternity litter that has to be handled as a family, or insulation contaminated wall-to-wall all add time and material. Historic Haddonfield work can involve slate, copper flashing, and a chimney older than the town's water system; the quote separates the animal work from the masonry so the owner sees both clearly. The inspection sorts your house into one of those buckets and the written quote shows exactly which items drive the number.

Haddonfield.wildlife_intro:
Haddonfield is a borough of historic houses and strict appearances: Colonials and Victorians along Kings Highway and the numbered streets, deep lots, old trees, and the Cooper River and Crows Woods closing off the east side. The housing's age is the animals' opportunity. Chimneys that predate caps, slate and shake roofs with a century of patched flashing, and carriage houses converted to garages all offer entries. Raccoons and squirrels lead the call log, bats hold several of the big old attics, and skunks commute from Crows Woods into the gardens nightly.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. Haddonfield work respects the architecture: caps and flashing details are matched to historic rooflines, and the plan is written so a preservation-minded owner can approve every visible piece.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Winslow Township foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. Winslow's sandy soil digs like a garden bed, and a burrow system here can run under a whole shed row in a season; the trapping plan covers every entrance, not the one the homeowner found first. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

faqs.q: What snakes turn up around Winslow Township, and which are dangerous?
faqs.a: This is Pine Barrens snake country. The northern pine snake — state-Threatened, a burrower in sandy soil — is the species people meet most dramatically, and it is protected: identification and referral, never handling. A separate southern population of timber rattlesnakes also persists in the Barrens. Around Cedar Brook and Blue Anchor the big snake in the woodpile is most often a pine snake; impressive, loud, protected, and best left to be photographed from a respectful distance. Common harmless residents include black racers, garter snakes, and eastern hognose, which plays dead theatrically. Non-listed snakes found inside a home can be caught and released outdoors within 200 meters.

Winslow Township.wildlife_intro:
Winslow is Camden County's big rural township, thirty-eight square miles of it, much of it Pine Barrens: Sicklerville's subdivisions in the north, farm and crossroads country through Blue Anchor and Cedar Brook, and state forest pressing in everywhere else. Housing runs from vinyl colonials to farmhouses and hunting-camp cabins, and the wildlife is Barrens wildlife. Groundhogs dig the sandy field edges, raccoons and bats take the farmhouses, skunks live under every other outbuilding, and pine snakes and black racers cross the sand roads all summer.

On farm and acreage properties the house is only part of the job. Barns shelter raccoon families in haylofts, groundhogs undermine run-in sheds and fence lines, and skunks take up residence under equipment sheds where they are discovered by smell. We plan the property as a whole — which structures to proof, which burrows to treat, where trapping effort actually pays — instead of chasing one animal at a time. Grain and feed storage gets the same attention as the house foundation, because spilled feed is usually what drew the animals to the buildings in the first place. Winslow jobs are planned property-wide, house, barn, and woodpile together, because in Barrens country the animals treat the whole parcel as one address.
